Zcash's NU7 upgrade activates today, and it makes blocks 3x faster.

What changes, per @ZcashFoundation and @Zcash:
- Blocks every 25 seconds instead of 75
- A Network Sustainability Mechanism sends 60% of transaction fees into a reserve. The 21M cap and halving schedule stay the same
- Old v4 transactions are switched off

The catch: v4 was the only way to move funds out of Sprout, Zcash's original shielded pool. About 12,200 ZEC is still in there, and it becomes unspendable unless a future upgrade reopens it.

@MidnightNtwrk's take yesterday: "If you like Zcash, you'll love Midnight." 

The honest version of that comparison:

- Zcash is private money. Shielded payments hide the sender, the recipient and the amount
- Midnight is programmable privacy. Smart contracts combine public on-chain state with private state that stays on your machine, and you choose what to disclose
- Both run on zero-knowledge proofs. Zcash has been doing it in production for ten years
- Speed: after NU7, Zcash makes a block every 25 seconds. Midnight makes one about every 6 seconds. The designs differ: Zcash is proof of work and counts confirmations, while Midnight finalises blocks with GRANDPA

They're closer than they look. Zcash grew out of the Zerocash protocol, and IOG's private proof-of-stake research, Crypsinous, is built on Zerocash-style coins.

As a builder, Sprout is the lesson I'm keeping: privacy systems upgrade by retiring old pools, and anyone who doesn't migrate gets left behind. Plan the migration path on day one.

Private money or programmable privacy: which does crypto need more right now?

The US midterms were this week, and every election brings the same pitch: put voting on a blockchain.

The people who study election security keep saying no:

- The National Academies (2018): blockchain "does little to solve the fundamental security issues of elections." Malware on a voter's phone can change a vote before it ever reaches the chain
- MIT researchers including Ron Rivest (2021): blockchain voting keeps internet voting's problems (malware, zero-days, denial of service) and can add new ones

They're right. The useful part isn't the chain. It's the proof.

That part is already real. ElectionGuard, an open-source toolkit, runs alongside paper ballots and existing scanners. Each ballot is encrypted and gets a zero-knowledge proof that it's valid. Voters get a code to check their ballot was counted, and anyone can verify the tally without seeing a single vote. It has been used in US elections in Wisconsin, Idaho, Utah and Maryland.

Where Cardano and Midnight fit is on-chain governance, not the ballot box.

@Cardano already runs on-chain voting: ADA holders delegate their vote to DReps, who vote on treasury withdrawals and protocol changes. Every DRep vote and every delegation is stored on-chain for good.

In a democracy, your representative's vote is public and your ballot is secret. Cardano has the first half. The second half is where @MidnightNtwrk comes in:

- Selective disclosure: prove you're eligible without handing over your ID
- Builders are already shipping private-ballot contracts on Midnight: prove you're on the voter list without revealing which voter you are, a nullifier stops anyone voting twice, and only the tally is public

As a builder, that's where I'd start: DAO and governance votes, where the stakes are real but there's no national election riding on it.

Should Cardano keep DRep votes public but let holders delegate privately?

The $6.3B Binance hack started with an engineer searching for an AI coding tool.

@binance published its incident report yesterday. How the attackers got in:

- June: a wallet engineer searched for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer. Binance caught it and replaced the laptop, but the attackers had already learned who worked on the wallet team
- September: another engineer, whose job-site profile mentioned Binance, was approached for a "job". After two interview rounds, including a live video call, he ran the "assignment" repo on his work computer. It swapped a real dev tool for malware that security software didn't catch
- 20 Oct: from that machine, they used an internal AI tool to take over two more engineers' computers, including the wallet engineer from June. He had a container deployment token on his
- 29 Oct: that got them into Binance's internal wallet-signing service

Pausing withdrawals didn't stop it. They had used Ethereum's EIP-7702 to give their own contract partial control of a hot wallet. Because that wallet used MPC, there was no single key to revoke it quickly.

Binance says 98% of the stolen assets are replaced and $2.85B is frozen. It also says it stopped 57 other North Korea-linked attempts this year: fake job interviews, fake developer tools, poisoned packages, browser extensions, fake video-call apps.

What I'm taking from it as a builder who lives in AI tools, plugins and MCP servers:
- Install tools from the official site or repo, never from a search result
- Never run an interview or "test" repo on a machine that touches keys
- Read what a setup script does before you run it
- Keep signing on a separate device

Two @MidnightNtwrk lessons too. Midnight's write-up on phishing says attacks start with picking a target from what's visible. Here it was a job profile. And Nightmode also runs on MPC signers, so the question isn't just who holds the key shares. It's what can ask them to sign.

What's your rule before installing a new AI coding tool or MCP server?

@binance just used a zero-knowledge proof to show customers their money is there, four days after the largest crypto theft on record.

What happened:
- 29 Oct: about $6.3B was taken from Binance's hot wallets. The FBI attributed it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group
- Binance says it has replaced about 95% with its own funds, and withdrawals are reopening in phases
- 2 Nov: it completed a zero-knowledge proof for its 31 Oct snapshot. 10 assets, each backed at least 1:1
- Customers can run Binance's open-source verifier and check their own balance was counted, without seeing anyone else's

What it doesn't show: it covers only those 10 tokens, at one moment, and it isn't an independent audit. The next snapshot is 4 Nov, and that proof takes 40–50 hours.

Could @MidnightNtwrk have stopped the hack? No. The attackers abused Binance's own wallet-signing systems. That's a key management failure, and privacy doesn't fix it.

Where Midnight's approach does help:

1. Proving without a public wallet list. Binance's proof hides customer balances, but its reserves side still relies on a published list of its wallets. Research from 2015 (Provisions, co-authored by Dan Boneh) showed an exchange can prove solvency without revealing its addresses or its totals. Prove the claim, keep the data private: that's what Midnight is built around.

2. The second wave. Binance is now warning about scams aimed at customers waiting on withdrawals: fake proof-of-reserves sites, paid "recovery" offers, wallet approvals. Midnight's own write-up argues that public balances and transfers let attackers pick and time their targets. Shielded balances take that data away. They won't stop someone from signing a bad approval.

3. Privacy with screening. The attacker's wallet was funded through Tornado Cash. In the Sig Network design Midnight announced last week, the contract sets which deposits it accepts and credits only those that pass screening.

Proof of reserves used to be a niche idea. This week the biggest exchange used one to calm users after the biggest theft. That pattern shouldn't only show up after a crisis.

Would a ZK proof of reserves make you trust an exchange again, or is self-custody the only answer now?

@IOHK_Charles called Midnight a "VPN for DeFi." Here's what that means in practice, and where Midnight Passport fits.

What he said (Bonnie Blockchain interview, 20 Oct):
"you click the button in your wallet, go through Midnight, do your DeFi on SOL, ETH, or ADA, and from their perspective it's Midnight doing that TX on your behalf."

Midnight's president @F_ZK_Now used the same line a week earlier: "Midnight is the VPN for DeFi."

The VPN part: a VPN doesn't stop a website seeing a visit. It stops it seeing that the visit came from you. Same idea here.

How it works (Nightmode, built with @Sig_Network):
- A Midnight contract gets its own account on Ethereum
- A threshold of independent signers signs only what that contract asks for. No single signer can act alone
- Nothing is bridged or wrapped. The assets stay on Ethereum
- Ethereum sees one account swapping on Uniswap or lending on Aave. Amounts and timing stay public. Who is behind each trade stays shielded on Midnight

It's live on @MidnightNtwrk's stagenet today. EVM NightMode is on the roadmap for Q4 2026.

Where Passport fits, in my reading: Charles's "button in your wallet" needs an account normal people can use. Midnight Passport is Midnight's identity and wallet layer. Per its draft spec:
- No seed phrase. You open the account with a passkey
- Apps and AI agents get grants, not your keys: spend caps, one token, an expiry, an optional fixed recipient
- The account contract checks those limits on every call, and grants can be revoked
- Users never need to hold DUST. A sponsor pays the fees, or they swap for them

Honest note: Passport is still at spec stage. The SDK repo says development restarted on 15 Oct and no package exists yet. Passport SDK v1 is on the roadmap for Q4 2026, Passport v2 for Q1 2027.

Deep dive on the line from @MidnightNtwrk's roadmap I care about most as a builder: a Midnight MCP, due Q1 2027.

The problem first. Ask a general AI assistant for a Compact contract and it guesses. Midnight's own docs say Compact and the Midnight SDK are barely in AI training data, so assistants invent syntax and call functions that don't exist.

Compact also moves fast. The language went from version 0.22 in March to 0.27 in September. In March, NativePoint was renamed JubjubPoint, and code using the old name stopped compiling. An AI that learned from older examples keeps writing it.

What you can use today:
- Midnight Expert: Claude Code plugins from Midnight that write and review Compact, then check it against the real compiler
- Kapa MCP: answers grounded in Midnight's docs, inside your editor
- midnight-mcp: a community MCP server by Idris Olubisi that also checks code against the compiler

My stack right now: Claude Code + Midnight Expert + the Kapa MCP.

What's coming:
- Q4 2026: AI DevEx for builders, AI tools that understand Compact and help write and debug contracts
- Q1 2027: a production Midnight MCP, plus AI agents trained on Midnight

MCP is a standard way for AI tools to connect to outside systems. Midnight Expert is built for Claude Code today. The roadmap says the production MCP will let assistants like Claude Code and Cursor build, test and deploy Midnight apps with accurate, current knowledge.

What is ShieldVIN

ShieldVIN is a digital passport for a vehicle that anyone can check without being shown what is inside it.

A car's record only has value if strangers can trust it, a buyer, a recycler, an insurer, a border authority. It is also the sort of thing nobody should publish. A full history is commercially sensitive to whoever is selling and personally identifying to whoever has owned it. Put it online and you have solved the first problem by creating the second.

That tension is about to stop being ours alone. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1738 (https://t.co/g4OOOCumgc) every vehicle placed on the EU market will have to carry a Digital Circularity Vehicle Passport, identity, provenance, history and the environmental declarations that go with it. The regulation asks for a passport that can be checked. It does not ask for one that is public.

- Validators verify the proof in milliseconds

- Soundness — if it's false, you can't fake it
